newsitem.title: UK: BA, American to present alliance plan.
newsitem.headline: BA, American to present alliance plan.

text.p: American Airlines and British Airways Plc were expected to detail their application for U.S. approval of their planned transatlantic alliance on Friday.
The two companies have set a news conference in Washington at 1500 GMT, coinciding with the deadline for submissions on the issue to Britain's Office of Fair Trading.
"We're poised to file the application" for approval from the U.S. Department of Transportation and the Department of Justice, British Airways spokesman John Lampl said on Thursday.

The BA/American news conference ends a week of vocal lobbying of Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT) by rival U.S. airlines strongly opposed to the alliance, which they believe will limit competition on the key route between the U.S. and Britain and continental Europe.

Industry sources said the timing for a U.S. application could be related to news that Britain and the U.S. are to resume "open skies" trade talks early next month aimed at opening up the transatlantic airline market to free competition.
A British government official said the British Department of Transport's (DOT) negotiating team would travel to Washington for three days of formal talks starting on February 4.

BA and American have argued their deal will lead to greater competition because it will only go ahead if Britain and the U.S. agree open skies, allowing all U.S. airlines access to Heathrow, the most popular of Europe's transatlantic landfalls.
Under the current aviation agreement dating back to March 1991, only British Airways, Virgin Atlantic Airways, American and United Airlines are allowed to use Heathrow.

But open skies talks have repeatedly stalled in the past on complaints by U.S. carriers that Heathrow is so crowded that open access would be meaningless unless they were to be granted some of British Airways' 38 percent share of slots.
On Thursday, Continental Airlines Inc, Trans World Airlines Inc and UAL Corp's United Airlines all spoke out against the alliance.

Continental and United in London both called on the competition authorities in Britain to toughen up proposed conditions for approving the deal, and in particular said BA should give up more runway slots at London's Heathrow airport.

The core OFT proposal is that BA and American release a total of 168 weekly takeoff and landing slots at London's Heathrow airport to allow in new competition -- sufficient slots for 12 new daily return services.

But Continental said that it would require 20 takeoff and landing slots a day at Heathrow along with adequate ground handling facilities if it was to be able to mount effective competition on routes to New York and to Houston.
Chairman Gordon Bethune called the alliance between BA and American effectively the world's largest airline merger.
"BA and AA promise to deliver the ultimate transportation benefit but...this huge deal is as attractive to travellers as that last great wonder of the Atlantic, The Titanic," he said.
United said that it was telling the OFT that BA and American should give up the equivalent of 210 weekly takeoff and landing slots at Heathrow and that it should give them up for free.
"BA and American rather than the competing airlines, must pay the economic price for reducing competition in key markets," United said in a statement.
